say: A tailor, a baker, a pharmacist and a bus captain all measure things every day: metres and centimetres, kilograms and grams, litres and millilitres, dollars and cents, hours and minutes. Today we become Measure and Money Masters. Our two tricks: change to one unit, and draw a time line.
I will name an object and a number. You write the best unit on your whiteboard: m, cm, km, g, kg, ml or ℓ. Ready? A bus is 12 what long? Hold up! Now tell your partner why it is not 12 cm or 12 km.
Look at the menu card. Before you add anything: do you think you can buy pizza, wings and cupcakes with $20? Show thumbs up or down, then we will check.
stuck: Stuck on the punch: “How many millilitres do 8 friends drink? How many ml is 2 ℓ?”
Adding prices: “Change each price to cents, or add the dollars first and then the cents.”
Over $20: “Which item could you swap for a cheaper one?”
Ready for more: “Can you spend EXACTLY $20? Try two pizzas, or three punches and two cupcakes.”

say: “2 m 35 cm. 1 m is 100 cm, so 2 m is 200 cm. 200 and 35 more is 235 cm. Careful with 2 m 5 cm: that is 200 and 5, so 205 cm, not 25.”
“The flour bag has 2 kg 100 g. I change it to grams: 2100 g. Mum uses 850 g. 2100 − 850 = 1250 g. Now I change back: 1000 g is 1 kg, so 1 kg 250 g. I check: 1250 + 850 = 2100.”

“From 9:45 to 11:20. Time does not work like ordinary numbers, because an hour is 60 minutes, not 100. So I draw a time line and jump to the next o’clock: 15 minutes to 10:00, 1 hour to 11:00, 20 minutes to 11:20. Altogether 1 hour 35 minutes.”

do: Ask: “What did you change the units to? Why that unit?”
Ask: “Show me your time line. Where did you jump to the o’clock?”
Ask: “How do you know your change is right? Add it back on.”
stuck: Hint 1: “Change everything to the smaller unit first: cm, g, ml, ¢ or minutes.”
Hint 2: “Draw a time line. Jump to the next o’clock, then whole hours, then the minutes left.”
Hint 3: “For the 24-hour clock: after 12 noon, add 12 to the hour.”

say: “Which is longer: 3 m 5 cm or 350 cm? How do you know?”
“Why can we not just do 11.20 − 9.45 to find how long it is from 9:45 to 11:20?”
ask: “Which is longer: 3 m 5 cm or 350 cm? How do you know?”
350 cm is longer: 3 m 5 cm = 305 cm. Time is not like ordinary numbers: an hour has 60 minutes, not 100, so we count on with a time line (15 min + 1 h + 20 min = 1 h 35 min).

say: “Today you changed to one unit to compare and calculate, you planned a budget, and you drew time lines to count across the hour. Measure and Money Masters!”

p3l9-title.note: Objective: Change compound units (m and cm, kg and g, ℓ and ml, $ and ¢) to one unit to compare, add and subtract; plan a budget; find durations, start and end times by drawing a time line, in 12-hour and 24-hour time. Heuristics taught: (1) change to one unit; (2) draw a time line and jump to the next o’clock (taught in a short lesson after page 1). Materials: Party menu cards (one per pair), play money, a metre ruler or measuring tape, a kitchen scale and a measuring jug if available, a clock with movable hands, mini whiteboards. Online: Show the menu card on screen; children use paper and pencil. Pairs work in breakout rooms and type their best party plan in the chat. Time plan (90 minutes, with a named 3-minute float inside talk time): opening 0 to 1.5, sneak-peek puzzles 1.5 to 4.5 (own paper, nobody marked, one show-me for both), warm-up game 4.5 to 7.5 (two rounds) and three quick questions 7.5 to 10.5, explore 10.5 to 25.5 (a Go further what-if is on the explore slide from the start; pairs go to pre-assigned breakout rooms), teaching 25.5 to 34 (change to one unit; the time line is taught after page 1; click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 34 to 39, worksheet 39 to 70 (page 1 in pairs, short teaching, page 2 on their own, a 60-second self-check slide after each page; after question 3 of page 1 any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation; from minute 67 everyone chooses), talk time 70 to 78.5 (volunteers first, pass is fine), exit ticket 78.5 to 84.5, look back 84.5 to 87.5, stamp and close 87.5 to 90. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are open to every child; the tutor never announces who is on which page and invites the whole group, never one child. If the class is behind, children finish the last question of each page at home; the check slides cover it. SPINE: Today's tool is Make a table. Make a table, fill it row by row and look down the columns. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p3l9-tool.note: SPINE: Show for about 20 seconds, inside the opening. Today's tool is Make a table. Make a table, fill it row by row and look down the columns. Look for where you use it. Point at the card on page 1 of the workbook.

p3l9-warmcheck.note: Minutes 1.5 to 4.5. Sneak-peek puzzles: two small puzzles on ideas we have not learnt yet. Give about 1 minute for each puzzle, then say "say it" ONCE for both: children say both answers together on three (about 30 seconds); nothing is held up to the camera. SAY: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome and so is I do not know. Nobody is marked." Puzzle 1 is an ACCESS puzzle: any child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 is a thinking puzzle. Children write both answers on their own paper and say them together on three (once for both puzzles); nothing is held up to the camera. No private messages. Never answers read out, never "who got it?". Do not show the answers on the slide now. Puzzle 1 answer (tutor only): 1 m. Listen for: 1 m is 100 cm, and 100 is more than 90. Puzzle 2 answer (tutor only): 5:15 pm. Listen for: 3:45 + 1 h = 4:45. 15 minutes more makes 5:00, and 15 more makes 5:15. Come back to puzzle 2 at talk time: "Now we know the idea, how could it help?" (volunteers only). Invite the WHOLE group once, never one child; this is an invitation, not a ranking, and any child may choose Think harder or the Investigation after question 3 of page 1. Never announce who is on which page, and never split pairs unless both children agree.

p3l9-warm1.note: Minutes 4.5 to 7.5. Play TWO rounds of four cards (the top row, then the bottom row). Name that unit. Read each card aloud; children write the unit on whiteboards and say the answer together on three, then click to show (the cards reveal in order). Ask each time: "Why not the other units?" A bus is 12 m (12 cm is a finger, 12 km is a long trip). A pencil is 15 cm. An MRT ride of about 15 km. Rice 5 kg. An eraser about 20 g. Medicine 5 ml. A fish tank about 40 ℓ. A watermelon about 3 kg. Ready for more: "Put these in order: 1 m, 90 cm, 1 km." (90 cm, 1 m, 1 km). Watch for children who mix up mass and volume units (kg for a drink).

p3l9-warm2.note: Minutes 7.5 to 10.5. Read each aloud, give thinking time, take answers, then click to show. Answers: 1) 140 cm (100 + 40). 2) 3000 g. 3) 2050 ml: watch for 250 ml, the most common mistake; 2 ℓ is 2000 ml and 50 more. 4) 80 minutes (60 + 20), not 120. 5) 14:00 (2 + 12). Ask after 3: "Why is it not 250?" Three quick questions only; 4) 1 hour 20 minutes = 80 minutes (60 + 20, not 120) and 5) 2:00 pm = 14:00 are on the take-home box of the Go further page in the workbook.

p3l9-explore1.note: Minutes 10.5 to 21. Party planner. Two constraints only (at least 2 ℓ of punch, at least one food) and "spend as close to $20 as you can": that is about 7 minutes of pair work. Exactly $20 is the extension (it stays on the slide), not part of the task. Pairs use the menu card and play money (or paper). You may buy more than one of an item. Punch: 8 × 250 ml = 2000 ml = 2 ℓ, so 1 bottle is the least; the rule is "at least 2 ℓ of punch (any number of bottles) and at least one food". Let pairs try first; prompt with "How did you add the prices?" The prices are whole and half dollars, so every child can add them. There are 15 ways to spend exactly $20 with up to 4 of each item (tutor reference), e.g. pizza + 2 punch + cupcake ($8.50 + $6 + $5.50); wings + 2 curry puffs + 2 punch ($6 + $8 + $6); 2 pizzas + 1 punch ($17 + $3); 2 curry puffs + 4 punch ($8 + $12); 3 punch + 2 cupcakes ($9 + $11). Hint for exact $20: half dollars come from the pizza, cupcakes and balloons, so those must come in pairs of halves (an even number altogether). Online: share the menu on screen; pairs type their plan in the chat. GO FURTHER (on the slide from the start of explore, so nobody waits): 12 friends and $30: how many bottles of punch? Can you spend exactly $30? Answer: 12 x 250 ml = 3000 ml = 3 l, so 2 bottles (2 l each) at least. Yes, there are many ways, e.g. 2 punch + 3 cupcakes + 3 balloons ($6 + $16.50 + $7.50), or 2 curry puffs + 2 punch + 2 cupcakes + 2 balloons. Any pair may choose it as soon as their first task is done; do not say who is ready for it. Online: pairs are in pre-assigned breakout rooms (set up before the lesson, auto-move in and auto-close with a timer, about 45 seconds per move). Visit each breakout room at least once while the pairs work (about 1 minute per room).

p3l9-explore2.note: Minutes 21 to 25.5. Gather the pairs to answer. Answers: 1) 8 × 250 ml = 2000 ml = 2 ℓ: at least 1 bottle, more is allowed. 2) Open: changing to cents (890 + 315 = 1205¢) or adding dollars then cents both work. 3) Yes, there are 15 ways with up to 4 of each item (examples on the previous slide notes). Ask: "How do you know a plan is exactly $20?" Volunteers show their adding. Any group can look at the half dollars.

p3l9-teach1.note: Teach heuristic 1: change to one unit. Hold up a metre ruler: "This is 1 m, 100 cm." Point to the bar: 2 m is 200 cm, and 35 cm more is 235 cm. Click the three rows: each time, the big unit becomes the small unit and we add the rest. Click "Careful!": "How do I write 2 m 5 cm in cm? Some people write 25. Is that right? 2 m alone is 200 cm, so it is 205." Same for 3 kg 40 g = 3040 g, not 340 g. Click "Why?": "Once everything is in the same unit, the numbers behave like the numbers we already know." Going back: 1650 g = 1000 g + 650 g = 1 kg 650 g.

p3l9-we1.note: Worked example. Ask first: "Can we take 850 away from 100 g?" (Not without breaking the kilograms.) Click each step. Think-aloud: "I change the bag to grams: 2 kg is 2000 g, plus 100 is 2100 g. Now it is a normal take-away: 2100 − 850 = 1250 g. I change back: 1000 g of it is 1 kg, so 1 kg 250 g. I check by adding back: 1250 + 850 = 2100." Some children prefer to work in kg and g separately (renaming 1 kg as 1000 g): accept it, but show why one unit is less likely to go wrong.

p3l9-try1.note: Write it, say the answer together on three, then click. a) 400 + 9 = 409 (not 49). b) 2000 ml is 2 ℓ, 750 ml left. c) 3 m 5 cm = 305 cm, so 350 cm is longer by 45 cm. Ask a child to explain c: the "5" in 3 m 5 cm is only 5 cm.

p3l9-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) 2 m 5 cm written as 25 cm, or 3 kg 40 g as 340 g. (2) Subtracting times like normal numbers (11.20 − 9.45), or counting 100 minutes in an hour. (3) 24-hour clock: adding 12 to am times or to 12:30 pm; reading 17:00 as 7 pm (4) Budgets: adding the dollars and forgetting to carry the cents (85¢ + 90¢ = $1.75).

p3l9-break.note: Five minutes. Call out times; children make the hands with their arms. Mix in 24-hour times: 15:00 (3 o’clock), 18:00 (6 o’clock), 21:15 (quarter past 9). Online: children stay in view of the camera.

p3l9-teachbudget.note: Teach before worksheet page 1 (Q3). Click each step. Think-aloud: "An estimate tells me if it is close. $15.50 is too close to be sure, so I work it out exactly in cents: 685 + 450 = 1135, and 395 more is 1530 cents, $15.30. That is more than $15: 30 cents short." Last click: "To spend as much as I can, I start with the dearest things and check every pair in order." Do not do the worksheet question for them: it uses 3 things from 5.

p3l9-ws1.note: Minutes 40.5 to 56. Walk around. Ask "What unit did you change to?" and "How do you know?" before helping. Q3b (if time): check pairs are listing sets in an order, starting with the dearest items, not guessing. PAGE 1 CLOCK (40.5 to 56): about 2 minutes to hand out and get started, then pairs auto-move to their pre-assigned breakout rooms (about 45 seconds), about 12 minutes of pair work with the room timer on, and auto-close back to the main room (about 45 seconds). Visit each room once. Items not finished are finished at home; the check slide covers them.

p3l9-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains. Q1f: 4 × 65 = 260 cm; 300 − 260 = 40 cm. Q2: in grams 1000, 1003, 1030, 1300. Q3a: 785 + 690 + 550 = 2025¢. Q3b: book + puzzle = $14.75 leaves $5.25: the dearest thing that fits is the pen set ($4.60), total $19.35. Without that pair, the best is $17.95, so $19.35 is the most. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and tick the corrected page against the answer slide (nothing is held up to the camera). Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l9-teach2.note: Teach heuristic 2: draw a time line. Ask first: "How long is it from 9:45 to 11:20?" Collect guesses (someone may say 1 h 75 min or 2 h 25 min). Click the three jumps one at a time. Think-aloud: "From 9:45 I jump to the next o’clock: 15 minutes to 10:00. Then a whole hour to 11:00. Then 20 minutes to 11:20. Add the jumps: 15 + 20 = 35 minutes, and 1 hour." Click the "Why not" box: "If we subtract like normal numbers we treat an hour as 100 minutes. That is the trap." Show it on a real clock if you have one.

p3l9-we2.note: Worked example. Click step 1: "45 minutes is too big a jump from 2:50, it goes past the o’clock. So I split it: 10 minutes to reach 3:00, and 45 − 10 = 35 minutes left." Then click the jumps: 10 min, 1 h, 35 min (the last click also shows all the times). Then the answer. Check: "From 2:50 to 4:35 is 10 + 60 + 35 = 105 minutes, and 1 h 45 min is 60 + 45 = 105 minutes." In 24-hour time this is 16:35 (we learn that after the break).

p3l9-ws2.note: Children work alone (page 2 is a little shorter than the 7.5-minute window in other lessons: Q5 is the main item; Q4 and Q6 are if time). Note who needs a short catch-up. Q6 (if time): check children list ALL the bus times (adding 25 each time across the hour: 07:05 + 25 min = 07:30).

p3l9-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains. Q5a: 15 min to 4:00, 1 h to 5:00, 10 min to 5:10. Q5b: 25 min to 5:00, 25 min more: 5:25 pm. Q5c: back 1 h from 9:15 to 8:15, back 50 min more: 8:15 to 8:00 is 15 min, then 35 min: 7:25 pm. Q6 (if time): 06:40, 07:05, 07:30, 07:55, 08:20. b) 08:20 + 35 min = 08:55. The "latest bus to arrive by 08:30" question is a Think Harder item: 07:55 + 35 min = 08:30 exactly; the 08:20 bus is too late. SELF-CHECK, about 60 seconds: children correct their own page against these answers in a different colour and tick the corrected page against the answer slide (nothing is held up to the camera). Ask “how do you know?” on ONE question only. Do not go through every answer aloud.

p3l9-stretch.note: For children who choose Think harder. Answers: 1) 2 h 35 min: 20 min to 23:00, 1 h to 00:00 (midnight), 1 h to 01:00, 15 min to 01:15. 2) 5 km: one day is 1250 + 1250 = 2500 m; two days 5000 m = 5 km. 3) Two 1 ℓ cartons: $7.20 (one 1 ℓ and four small cartons cost $3.60 + $4.40 = $8.00; eight small cartons cost $8.80).

p3l9-challenge.note: SUPPORT FOR Q4 (if time; this replaces the old 24-hour-clock teaching slide), only for a child who chooses it: the 24-hour clock keeps counting after 12 noon: 13, 14 … 23, then midnight is 00:00. am: same numbers with 2 digits (6:05 am is 06:05). pm: add 12 to the hour (4:20 pm is 16:20); going back, take away 12 (19:30 is 7:30 pm). Careful: 12:45 pm stays 12:45. Quick check: 15:00 is 3 pm; 9:10 pm is 21:10. Use as a pair challenge or in talk time. Ask for the reason every time. Answers: 1) 300 g (half the water weighs 1200 − 750 = 450 g, so all the water is 900 g; the bottle is 1200 − 900 = 300 g). 2) $1.60 (take away the extra 60¢ on each file: $9.20 − $1.20 = $8.00 for 5 pens; 800¢ ÷ 5 = 160¢. A file costs $2.20. Check: $4.80 + $4.40 = $9.20).

p3l9-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried the Go further, or if they are stuck. The diagrams show the problem, not the answer. Ask: What do you notice? What changed between the two bottles? (Only the water.) For Q2: what would the bars show without the yellow parts? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p3l9-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried, with the "see it" slide. Q1: compare the two bottles: the bottle is the same, only the water changed, so the difference is half the water. Q2: the same idea as Lesson 4 (Model Makers): remove the extra parts so all the bars are equal. Change $8.00 to 800¢ before dividing.

p3l9-talk.note: Minutes 70 to 78.5. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Answers: 350 cm is longer, because 3 m 5 cm = 305 cm. An hour has 60 minutes, not 100, so we count on with a time line: 9:45 to 11:20 is 15 min + 1 h + 20 min = 1 h 35 min. Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME FLOAT: this part holds the lesson's named 3-minute float. If you are behind, shorten talk time (one discussion question, then the partner share); if you are on time, use the full time for the second question and the return to sneak-peek puzzle 2. Never take time from the exit ticket, look back or stamp. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a pass is always fine and so is sharing with a partner. No cold-calling by name, no public tallies or rankings, and nobody is told they were wrong in front of the group. Nobody is called on by name.

p3l9-exit.note: Minutes 78.5 to 84.5. Answer: 4:50 pm (3:30 + 30 min = 4:00, + 50 min = 4:50; or 1 h gives 4:30, + 20 min gives 4:50). A child who writes 4:90 is adding like normal numbers: revisit the time line next lesson. Extension: plan a real outing with a timetable and a $50 budget. Answers stay on the child’s own paper and are ticked against the answer slide. Never mark or read out answers in front of the group. Reflection (look back) follows on the next slide: allow 3 minutes, 2 for the children plus a short share.

p3l9-reflect.note: SPINE: Minutes 84.5 to 87.5. Start the timer (90 seconds). Say: "Pick one problem from today. Question 1: did I answer the question? Question 2: does my answer make sense? Question 3: can I check it another way? Tick, write one line, or pass. If you are still stuck, tick the box and I will come." Children tick the Look back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook, or just tick on paper. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share. Praise a check you saw, not speed. Then stamp the journals. After the look-back, minutes 87.5 to 90 are flex time (the buffer): finish stamps, then goodbye. Do not start anything new.
